newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Labour expects strong "no" in super vote.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Labour expects strong "no" in super vote.

text.p: The opposition New Zealand Labour Party expects voters to say "no" to compulsory superannuation savings in a referendum in September, its finance spokesman said on Thursday.
"The mood against it is likely to strengthen, rather than weaken as problems emerge," Michael Cullen said in a speech to a retirement savings summit.
"The Labour Party is working on the very strong assumption that the New Zealand voters will be sensible enough to vote no," Cullen said.
Recent polls have indicated strong opposition to the principle of a compulsory savings scheme to replace the current universal pension scheme.
A TV3 poll on Wednesday showed 63 percent opposed to the idea of compulsory pension savings.
The precise shape of the proposed will be released in July, but Treasurer Winston Peters has sketched the likely outline of the proposal.
Cullen said at the heart of the problem a humane society could not avoid the state being the final guarantor of an adequate standard of living, and this was at odds with compulsory private savings.

He said there was no proof such a scheme would lift the national savings rate, and it could even lower it. It would divert savings away from farm and business development and away from the repayment of mortgages, decreasing the overall efficiency of savings.
Indications from Peters that those who had not saved enough would receive a top-up would impose enormous fiscal risks on the state, Cullen said.

He said spending on superannuation would bottom out at 4.8 percent of GDP in five years, and the demographic trends were made to look worse by recent falls in the percentage of GDP spent on superannuation.
"This very low base -- barely half the average of the OECD at the present time -- makes the rise to a little over 10 percent of GDP at peak in forty years time look much steeper."
Cullen said sustained migration at 15,000 a year and productivity growth of two percent a year would improve the key numbers.
"There are things that we can do which are feasible policy responses that are far less of a leap in the dark than the proposed savings scheme."
Labour's policy was to maintain the current superannuation scheme, but pre-fund some of the future obligations through applying a proportion of taxation to a specific pension fund.
"The next fifteen to twenty years provides an enormously favourable fiscal and demographic window of opportunity to do this," Cullen said.

He said the superannuation accord, signed by Labour, the left-wing Alliance and the conservative National Party in 1993 to take the pension debate out of the political arena, but rejected by Peters' New Zealand First, would be hard to resurrect.

"At the moment it is in a state of suspension. But the recent history does not make me optimistic that my colleagues will see it as their role to ride in to the rescue yet again. We are tired of moral victories," Cullen said.
He said it would be more likely Labour would pursue its own policy "and be damned to those who at heart do not really believe in the state's primary role in the provision of retirement income".
